title: What the server does for an admin navigation
headline: All 12 findings of the audit stand (8 confirmed, 4 corrected) and this pass added three; none argues for removing, hiding or merging a feature, and none rests on a table being empty. The admin's lists, streaming and cache tags are well made: the waste is in the shell and the home screens, and it is paid per owner tab and per save, so it grows with stores and owners, not with data. Three numbers tell it: building the store menu costs 125 ms of blocking CPU on every shell render (220 permission lookups; 0.1 ms once memoised), the shell is rendered again after every save and at least 39 save sites render the whole route twice because the browser asks again, and a store Home view runs 29 to 46 statements before its first content. Before opening is the cheap time: do the menu memo (AD-1), the double redraws (AD-13), the hidden-tab polls (AD-9), the products list's unused reads (AD-7) and a statement counter so this cannot grow unseen again (AD-12) first.

findings.title: The store menu is rebuilt with 220 slow permission lookups on every shell render
findings.evidence: matchPath() filters the 416-page table and sorts the 264 store pages on every call, and the sort runs a regex twice per comparison (pageParams). The layout calls storeTabs() and storeAreas(); each runs storeSections(), which asks canOpenPath() -> permissionOfPath() -> matchPath() for all 110 menu items. My own run in Node 22: 220 lookups for 110 distinct paths and 125 ms per build with every feature on. The skeptic measured 121 to 125 ms (every feature), 101 to 112 ms (shop only), 60 ms (a website), 243 ms (a store that is not open: two lookups per item, layout.tsx:82), 0.46 to 0.53 ms per matchPath() call of which the filter and sort are 0.46 ms, and 0.1 ms for the whole build once the lookup is memoised by path. The answer depends only on the code and the member's keys. The shell is rendered on a hard load, after every save that calls refresh() (599 sites) and on every router.refresh(), not on a soft navigation.
findings.cost: 100 to 125 ms of blocking CPU per store shell render for a shop, 60 ms for a website, 243 ms for a suspended or closed store (measured on this machine). 64 ms more on the Settings and Website hub pages (one storeSections() pass, the skeptic's measure). About 130 ms per pass when the AI manager filters the 264 store pages (estimate: 264 times 0.5 ms). It is synchronous, so the instance serves nothing else meanwhile. Today only the team pays it; it multiplies with every owner's saves once stores open (estimate: 1,000 saves cost about 2 minutes of CPU).
findings.who_pays: The server per shell render (function CPU), and the owner, who waits for it on every hard load, every save and every progress poll tick.

findings.title: Every admin request from a session without two-step calls Supabase Auth
findings.evidence: readSession() verifies the token, reads the account row, then for an aal1 session calls supabase.auth.getUser() over HTTP to list factors, on every request (React's cache spans one render only). Every page render, server action, notice poll and admin route handler goes through it. A save pays it twice: once in the action's guard and once in the redraw that follows, which is a new render with a new cache. The writes that follow run only on a mismatch or while the break-glass switch is on. One more thing found in this pass and not checked against production: getClaims() itself verifies locally only when the project signs tokens with an asymmetric key; for an HS256 token it falls back to getUser() (GoTrueClient.js:5537-5544), which is one more HTTP call per request for every session, with or without two-step. The test stand-in signs with HS256 and says so (auth-stub.mjs:3). Which kind production's project uses is not in the repo.
findings.cost: One extra HTTP round trip per admin request for every account without a second factor, two per save, one per 60-second notice poll. Not timed here; the code review rates it severity 2. If production still signs with the shared secret, every admin request of every session makes one more. It grows with every owner who signs in without two-step once stores open.
findings.who_pays: The server per request and the owner on every navigation and save.
fix_steps: First look, by a person with access: in the Supabase dashboard of project ybsozesfuxuitoacntfo, Authentication, JWT signing keys. If tokens are still signed with the legacy shared secret (HS256), move to an asymmetric signing key (Supabase's own migration; no code change: getClaims() then verifies with the cached key set, fetched once per instance per 10 minutes). Record which it was in docs/decisions.md.

findings.title: Nothing counts what a screen costs the server, so the Home grew to 30 statements unseen
findings.evidence: The admin has budgets for scripts (seven screens in admin-scripts.spec.ts) and ratchets for unchecked reads, but no count of statements or server time per screen. The skeptic's search of src and docs for a statement or query budget, a per-request counter or Server-Timing found none. control-center.ts states its own rule ('a handful of queries, never per store') in a comment and has since grown to 21 statements plus per-store reads, with nothing to notice it. The admin's speed beacon reports TTFB, which with a static shell says nothing about the data behind it. With no real traffic yet, production's statistics cannot show it either. Every statement the app sends goes through one pool made in src/db/client.ts:63-80, so one place can count them all.
findings.cost: No running cost of its own. It is why AD-1, AD-2, AD-6, AD-7 and AD-14 were not seen: each feature added one more read to a shared screen.
findings.who_pays: Everyone later: the owner in wait, the database in load, the team in audits like this one.
fix_steps: Step 1, the counter. src/db/client.ts create(): wrap the pool's query so each statement adds one to the store of an AsyncLocalStorage when one is running, and nothing otherwise. Export countStatements(run) that runs a function inside a fresh store and returns { result, statements, ms }. It counts; it never keeps a statement's text or values (D400).

Step 2, the log line. For renders, where the app cannot wrap the request: a per-render counter from React cache() (cache(() => ({ statements: 0, started: Date.now() }))) that the same wrapper also bumps; in src/app/admin/(gated)/layout.tsx's Gate, take the object and log one line in after(): log('info', 'admin.render', { statements, ms }) through src/server/log.ts. Outside a render cache() returns a fresh object each call, so jobs and routes are unaffected.

Step 3, the budget. A new src/server/admin-statements.int.test.ts runs, against the seeded store and its owner, the loaders of five screens inside countStatements(): the store shell (storeShellData of AD-4), the store Home (controlCenter for one store, getSetupProgress, demoContent), the orders list (resolveOrderList, listOrdersPage, listOrderViews, tagSuggestions), the products list for an editor, and the platform Home's five loaders. It compares each count to src/server/admin-statements.baseline.json and fails when one rises, and when one falls until the baseline is lowered, exactly as ratchet.scan.test.ts does with scripts/ratchet.mjs.
Step 4, the menu. The count test of AD-1 (canOpen called at most once per menu item) is the menu's budget.

Step 5, the rule. One paragraph in docs/performance.md beside the first-scripts budgets, and a line in CLAUDE.md's Conventions: a change that adds a read to the shell or to a home screen raises a number in the baseline and says why in its commit.
Order: step 1 before the other findings (they measure with it); write the baseline with today's numbers, then let each fix lower them.

src/server/ratchet.scan.test.ts and scripts/ratchet.mjs are the pattern to copy.

findings.title: At least 39 saves draw the whole route twice: the action redraws it, then the browser asks again
findings.evidence: A server action that calls refresh() answers with the route already drawn again: refresh() sets pathWasRevalidated (revalidate.js:67-77), so the action handler does not skip page rendering (action-handler.js:926-935). In many client parts the code then calls router.refresh() as well, which sends a second request that renders every layout and the page once more. Counted in this pass: 90 router.refresh() calls in 50 files of src/components/admin and src/app/admin. A static pass (script in the scratch folder) resolved the action awaited just before each call and read its body: at 36 sites every candidate action already calls refresh(); 6 are mixed; at 11 the action does not refresh, so the client call is needed; 37 were not resolved (polls, fetches to route handlers, helpers), and 3 of those are doubles by hand, which makes 39. Reading both sides by hand confirmed nine: stock adjust and policy (inventory-table.tsx:139 and 151 with inventory/actions.ts:23 and 31), locations (locations-view.tsx:92, 115, 128: all 6 actions of locations/actions.ts refresh), the product passport (passport-editor.tsx:32 with passport/actions.ts:15), an automation rule, a discount and a campaign. The last three and the cart reminder do router.push(back) and then router.refresh(): three renders for one save (the editor being left, the list, the list again). No written rule or scan test says which side refreshes (rg over docs/rules and the scan tests).
findings.cost: One whole-route render more than needed on each of these saves, two more where an editor pushes and refreshes: the guard's 2 statements (and an Auth call for a session without two-step, AD-3), the shell (100 to 125 ms of CPU until AD-1, 6 statements until AD-4, 51 to 66 KB until AD-5) and all of the page's own reads. Stock adjustments, redirects, suppliers, imports and moving in from another shop are among them: things an owner does many times in a row.
findings.who_pays: The server and the database per save; the owner's browser, which parses the route twice; the owner, who sees the page settle twice.

The four editors that push and refresh (discount-editor.tsx:126-127, campaign-editor.tsx:169-170, automation/rule-editor.tsx:208-209, reminder-editor.tsx:116-117): keep router.push(back) and drop router.refresh(). findings.title: The pages and articles lists read and check every page's whole content, twice, to show a title and a state
findings.evidence: listPages() selects draft and published, the two whole JSON documents of a page, for every page of a type, with no limit (pages.ts:136-140). In code each row is parsed twice with the full page schema (parsePageContent, a zod parse of a 4,300-line schema file) and the two results are compared with JSON.stringify to tell 'published' from 'changed' (pages.ts:112-115, page-content.ts:4317-4319). The list then shows a title, an address, a state, two dates, two flags and a thumbnail. Timed in this pass on ten real page documents from the themes (average 8.3 KB of JSON): 0.64 ms of blocking CPU per row, so 19 ms for 30 pages and 128 ms for 200 articles, with about 16.6 KB per row read from the database (3.3 MB for 200). The same view serves pages, articles, headers, footers and product layouts (views.tsx:66) and the platform's own pages (platform/pages/views.tsx:57). Five callers want only an id, a title or an address (pages/actions.ts:408, platform/pages/actions.ts:332, try/[sandbox]/actions.ts:219, shopify-copy.ts:555, articles/blogs/page.tsx:32), and the Admin API's list filters by date after reading everything (admin-api-content.ts:222). The view then awaits its other reads one after another with no Suspense, 4 to 6 by type (views.tsx:68, 76, 79, 124, then 138-139, or 145 and 162, or 179-180), and siteLayoutChoice() is read twice for headers and footers (145, 162). The first of them, storePageContext() (pages/context.ts:79-110), builds the page builder's whole context, with menu previews, every field group and their lookups in sequence, and the list uses two things from it: siteBase and the duplicate action (views.tsx:150 and 155).
findings.cost: Per list view: two documents per page from the database and 0.64 ms of CPU per page, growing without bound with a store's pages and above all its articles. A blog moved in from Shopify or WordPress has hundreds of posts on day one. Today's pages are the team's demo content (1,389 rows, 9.1 MB in production), so nothing shows yet.
findings.who_pays: The database (rows and bytes), the server (a synchronous parse that holds the instance), and the owner, who waits for the list.
